summary: This note traces the meaning and history of the term 'Near East' and how different organizations have defined it. It covers the origins of the term in the Levant trading companies of Elizabeth I's era, how 'Middle East' largely displaced it, and how the UN, UNESCO, FAO, the UK Foreign Office, the US State Department, USAID, Encyclopaedia Britannica and National Geographic each define the region. It also notes that 'Near East' means something different in ancient studies and that the US is the chief remaining nation officially using the term.
one_line: Explains the shifting meaning of the term 'Near East' and how various agencies and institutions define the region today.
key_facts: Elizabeth I of England chartered the Company of Merchants of the Levant, known as the Levant Company, in 1581.
In 1582 the ship The Great Susan transported the first ambassador, William Harebone, to the Ottoman Porte at Constantinople.
The East India Company was chartered in 1600 for trade to the East Indies.
'Near East' fell into disgrace in diplomatic and military circles, and 'Middle East' prevailed as the preferred term.
The United Nations Statistics Division defines Western Asia to contain the countries included elsewhere in the Middle East.
The Food and Agriculture Organization describes its entire theatre of operations as the Near East, but assigns Cyprus, Malta and Turkey to both the European and Near Eastern regions.
UNESCO recognizes neither a Near East nor a Middle East, dividing countries among Arab States, Asia and the Pacific, and Africa.
The United States is described as the chief remaining nation to assign official responsibilities to a region called the Near East.
The U.S. Agency for International Development does not use the term Near East, and its definition of Middle East corresponds to that of the State Department.

The Encyclopædia Britannica's Near East includes Armenia, Azerbaijan, Bahrain, Cyprus, Egypt, Georgia, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Libya, Oman, Palestine, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Sudan, Syria, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, the West Bank, and Yemen.
According to the National Geographic Society, the terms Near East and Middle East denote the same territories.
In 1855 Thomas Taylor Meadows, an 'official Chinese interpreter of 10 years' active service', wrote a letter reprinted in Littel's Living Age.
In the ancient sense, 'Near Eastern Languages' includes Sumerian and Akkadian, while in the modern sense it likely means any or all of the Arabic languages.
The Triple Entente and the Triple Alliance, the latter formed in 1882, were in part a cause of World War I.

entities.name: Elizabeth I of England
entities.role: English monarch who was primarily interested in trade with the east and chartered the Levant Company

entities.name: Company of Merchants of the Levant
entities.role: trading company chartered in 1581, shortened to Levant Company and also known as The Turkey Company

entities.name: The Great Susan
entities.role: ship that transported the first ambassador, William Harebone, to Constantinople in 1582

entities.name: William Harebone
entities.role: first ambassador sent to the Ottoman Porte at Constantinople

entities.name: Ottoman Porte
entities.role: government of the Ottoman Empire at Constantinople

entities.name: East India Company
entities.role: company chartered in 1600 for trade to the East Indies

entities.name: Alfred Thayer Mahan
entities.role: American diplomatic and military figure concerned about naval vulnerability of trade routes in the Persian Gulf and Indian Ocean

entities.name: United Nations
entities.role: body that formulates multiple regional divisions for its various operations

entities.name: UNICEF
entities.role: UN agency that recognizes the 'Middle East and North Africa' region

entities.name: UNESCO
entities.role: UN agency that recognizes neither a Near East nor a Middle East, dividing countries among three regions

entities.name: United Nations Statistics Division
entities.role: defines Western Asia to contain the countries included elsewhere in the Middle East

entities.name: Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO)
entities.role: UN agency that describes its entire theatre of operations as the Near East

entities.name: Foreign and Commonwealth Office
entities.role: United Kingdom office that recognises a Middle East and North Africa region but not a Near East

entities.name: State Department
entities.role: US government body most influential in promulgating the Near Eastern regional system and officially preferring the term Near East

entities.name: U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID)
entities.role: independent US agency under the Department of State that does not use the term Near East

entities.name: Encyclopædia Britannica
entities.role: reference work that defines the Near East as including 23 listed countries and territories

entities.name: National Geographic Society
entities.role: organization stating that Near East and Middle East denote the same territories

entities.name: Thomas Taylor Meadows
entities.role: author of an 1855 letter, a member of the Oriental Club, who was an official Chinese interpreter

entities.name: Littel's Living Age
entities.role: publication that reprinted Meadows's 1855 letter

entities.name: The Times
entities.role: newspaper to which Meadows's letter was earlier sent

entities.name: Triple Entente
entities.role: alignment of powers that was in part a cause of World War I

entities.name: Triple Alliance
entities.role: alliance formed in 1882 that was in part a cause of World War I

entities.name: World War I
entities.role: war partly caused by the Triple Entente and Triple Alliance, ending in 1918
